title: Coach for the next level, not just this one
body: If you only give feedback on today's job, you are preparing people to stay exactly where they are.

title: Growing yourself, then others
body: Before you are a leader, success is all about growing yourself. When you become a leader, success is all about growing others.
author: Jack Welch

title: First-time manager readiness
body: A strong individual contributor wants to move into management but has never led anyone. What is the best next step?

options.label: Promote them into a team lead role immediately
Give them a bounded leadership rep first — leading a project, onboarding a hire — then debrief it together
Tell them to wait for a formal opening
Send them to a management training course

explanation: A bounded rep with a real debrief tests the aptitude and builds the skill before the stakes (and the org chart) are permanent.

title: Promoted for tenure
body: A high performer was promoted to manager purely for seniority, having never led anyone. Six months later the team was worse off, and the company had lost a strong individual contributor while gaining a struggling manager. Management is a different job, not a reward for doing the old one well.

title: Ask about two years from now
body: In your next 1:1, ask: 'what skill do you want to be known for in two years?' Write down the answer and revisit it in 90 days.

title: Give feedback within 48 hours
body: The further feedback drifts from the moment, the less specific and less useful it becomes — for praise and for correction alike.

title: Your job is to make yourself replaceable
body: A manager who is the only one who can do a task has not built a team — they have built a bottleneck with a title.

title: Test potential with real stakes
body: Before promoting for potential, give a real stretch assignment with real consequences and see how they handle ambiguity — not just how they perform with you supervising closely.

title: Praise the decision, not just the outcome
body: A good decision that did not work out still deserves recognition — otherwise people learn to optimize for safe bets instead of good judgment.

title: The promotion that never came because no one asked
body: A talented engineer kept getting passed over for promotion because their manager assumed they weren't interested in management. Nobody had ever actually asked. Ambition changes — don't guess at it, ask directly and often.

title: Separate "ready for more scope" from "ready for the title"
body: Scope can expand gradually. Titles tend to be binary and political. Give the scope first, and let the title catch up once the case is undeniable.

title: Tell them you'd hate to lose them
body: Write down, honestly, who on your team you'd be most afraid to lose. Then ask yourself when you last actually told them that.

title: A growth plan without a deadline is a wish
body: "Get better at X" is not a plan. "Lead the migration project by Q2, debrief after" is.

title: Excellent work, silent in the room
body: A report consistently delivers excellent work but never speaks up in group settings. What is the highest-leverage move?

options.label: Mark them down on "communication" in the performance review
Create lower-stakes settings for them to practice speaking up, and coach it as a learnable skill
Assume they are not leadership material
Speak for them in meetings so their ideas still get heard

explanation: Treating quietness as a fixed trait writes someone off. Treating it as a learnable skill, practiced in lower-stakes settings first, is both kinder and usually more accurate.

title: Your best people leave the way they stay — on purpose
body: Regularly ask high performers what would make them consider leaving. Waiting for the resignation letter to ask is already too late.
